level1.intro.subject: program
level1.intro.text: You typed {lines} and clicked Run. At this level your program is still just text, as you wrote it. Your computer stores it as [[byte|bytes]], which the next zoom level shows. Highlighted words, like that one, open a short explanation.

level1.size.subject: program
level1.size.text: Your program has {lines} and {characters}, counting the spaces and the invisible [[newline|newline]] at the end of each line.

level2.intro.subject: program
level2.intro.text: A computer can’t store letters as such: it stores [[byte|bytes]], numbers from 0 to 255. So each character of your program becomes a number, or a few numbers, using an agreement called [[utf8|UTF-8]]. Even the spaces at the start of a line, and the ends of lines, are stored.

level2.caption.subject: program
level2.caption.text: Your program in bytes: {bytes}, shown line by line, the same bytes a file of it would hold. Each box shows the byte in hexadecimal, then as an ordinary number. Select one to see its character.

byte.character.subject: byte
byte.character.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.character.text: Every character has an agreed number. **{char}** is {value}. This agreement is called [[utf8|UTF-8]], and for English letters and common symbols, each character takes exactly one [[byte|byte]].

byte.multiByte.subject: byte
byte.multiByte.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {charBytes}
byte.multiByte.text: Every character has an agreed number, but only English letters and common symbols fit in one [[byte|byte]]. [[utf8|UTF-8]] stores **{char}** as {charSize}: **{charBytes}**. This byte is the {placeInChar} of them.

byte.newline.subject: byte
byte.newline.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.newline.text: The [[newline|newline]] at the end of line {line}. You can’t see it, but it is stored as number **{value}**, and it tells Python the line is over.

byte.indent.subject: byte
byte.indent.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.indent.text: One of the {indent} that indent line {line}. Indentation is stored like any other character, as number **{value}**, and for Python it matters: it says which lines belong together.

byte.indentOneSpace.subject: byte
byte.indentOneSpace.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.indentOneSpace.text: The space that indents line {line}. Indentation is stored like any other character, as number **{value}**, and for Python it matters: it says which lines belong together.

byte.quote.subject: byte
byte.quote.title: Byte {number} of {count}: **{char}** is stored as {value}
byte.quote.text: A quote mark is stored like any other character. Python uses the pair of them to find where a piece of text starts and ends.

byte.bits.subject: byte
byte.bits.title: How the number {value} is stored
byte.bits.text: A byte is 8 [[bit|bits]]: 8 tiny on/off switches. Each switch has a value, shown under it. Add up the values of the switches that are on, and you get the number. This way of counting is called [[binary|binary]].

byte.bitsPattern.subject: byte
byte.bitsPattern.text: So **{char}** is stored as the pattern **{bits}**.

byte.bitsPatternMultiByte.subject: byte
byte.bitsPatternMultiByte.text: So the {placeInChar} byte of **{char}** is stored as the pattern **{bits}**.

level3.intro.subject: program
level3.intro.text: To understand code, Python first needs its words, just as you read words rather than single letters. So it [[encoding|decodes]] your {bytes} into text and picks out the meaningful pieces, called [[token|tokens]]. In Python, indentation matters, so the tokens also mark where an indented block starts and ends.

level3.caption.subject: program
level3.caption.text: Your program, line by line, as the {tokens} Python found. Select one to see what it is.

level3.encoding.subject: program
level3.encoding.text: **ENCODING** comes before line 1: Python’s note that it read your bytes as **{encoding}**. It isn’t part of your code.

token.name.subject: token
token.name.title: **{text}** is a name
token.name.text: Python has read the letters of **{text}** and decided they form one word: a **name**. It doesn’t know yet what the name means.

token.keyword.subject: token
token.keyword.title: **{text}** is a keyword
token.keyword.text: **{text}** is a keyword: a name reserved by Python, which you can’t use for your own things. The tokenizer still calls it a **NAME**; working out that it’s special comes next.

token.openBracket.subject: token
token.openBracket.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.openBracket.text: An opening bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.closeBracket.subject: token
token.closeBracket.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.closeBracket.text: A closing bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.openSquare.subject: token
token.openSquare.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.openSquare.text: An opening square bracket. It starts a list, as in [1, 2], or picks something out, as in names[0]. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.closeSquare.subject: token
token.closeSquare.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.closeSquare.text: A closing square bracket. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.colon.subject: token
token.colon.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.colon.text: A colon. After if, for, def and the like, it says the block they control comes next. Colons have other jobs too, as in dictionaries and slices. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.comma.subject: token
token.comma.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.comma.text: A comma: it separates things, such as the items of a list, or what a function is given. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.equals.subject: token
token.equals.title: **{text}** is punctuation
token.equals.text: An equals sign. In a line like x = 1, the name on its left gets the value on its right. The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.op.subject: token
token.op.title: **{text}** is punctuation or an operator
token.op.text: The tokenizer calls every piece of punctuation, and every operator such as + or ==, **OP**, short for operator, and notes the exact kind: **{exactType}**.

token.number.subject: token
token.number.title: **{text}** is a number
token.number.text: Python has read **{text}** and decided it is one number. Working out its value comes later.

token.string.subject: token
token.string.title: **{text}** is one piece of text
token.string.text: The whole text is one token, quote marks included. Python saw the opening quote mark and kept reading until the closing one.

token.comment.subject: token
token.comment.title: A comment
token.comment.text: Everything from **#** to the end of the line is a comment, written for people. The tokenizer keeps it as a token, but Python ignores it from here on.

token.newline.subject: token
token.newline.title: End of line {line}
token.newline.text: This token comes from byte 10, the invisible [[newline|newline]]. It tells Python the line of code is complete.

token.noCode.subject: token
token.noCode.title: A line with no code
token.noCode.text: Line {line} has no code on it. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but no line of code. Python ignores it from here on.

token.commentLine.subject: token
token.commentLine.title: End of a comment line
token.commentLine.text: Line {line} holds only a comment. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but no line of code. Python ignores it from here on.

token.insideBrackets.subject: token
token.insideBrackets.title: A line break inside brackets
token.insideBrackets.text: Line {line} ends inside brackets, so the line of code goes on to the next line. Its newline becomes an **NL** token, not a NEWLINE, and Python ignores it from here on.

token.indent.subject: token
token.indent.title: A block starts
token.indent.text: Line {line} starts with {indent}, deeper than the line of code before it, so a block starts here. In Python, indentation is part of the meaning.

token.dedent.subject: token
token.dedent.title: A block ends
token.dedent.text: An empty token: line {line} starts further left, at column {column}, so an indented block has ended. Each block that ends gets its own DEDENT.

token.dedentAtEnd.subject: token
token.dedentAtEnd.title: A block ends
token.dedentAtEnd.text: An empty token: line {line} doesn’t exist, the file has ended, so an indented block has ended. Each block that ends gets its own DEDENT.

token.endmarker.subject: token
token.endmarker.title: End of the file
token.endmarker.text: An empty token with no characters at all. Python adds it when the file runs out, so it knows it has seen everything.

token.other.subject: token
token.other.title: A token tokenize calls {type}
token.other.text: The tokenizer calls this piece of your code a **{type}**.

token.whereLines.subject: token
token.whereLines.text: **Where:** from line {line} to line {endLine}. tokenize writes this as **{position}**.

level4.intro.subject: program
level4.intro.text: Words alone don’t say what goes with what. So Python works out the [[structure|structure]]: which pieces belong together, which lines belong inside which block, and what each line does, recorded as boxes inside boxes.

level4.caption.subject: program
level4.caption.text: Your program as the {boxes} Python made, each inside the box that holds it. Select one to see its role.

level4.noTree.subject: program
level4.noTree.text: Python couldn’t work out the structure of your program, because it has a syntax error. The Terminal shows where.

level4.signposts.subject: program
level4.signposts.title: Where did the brackets, colons and indentation go?
level4.signposts.text: They were signposts. Brackets showed which pieces go together, and colons and indentation showed which lines belong inside a block. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.signpostsBrackets.subject: program
level4.signpostsBrackets.title: Where did the brackets go?
level4.signpostsBrackets.text: They were signposts, showing which pieces go together. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.signpostsBlocks.subject: program
level4.signpostsBlocks.title: Where did the colons and indentation go?
level4.signpostsBlocks.text: They were signposts. Colons and indentation showed which lines belong inside a block. The boxes now show that directly, by sitting inside each other, so the signposts are no longer needed.

level4.notDrawn.subject: node
level4.notDrawn.text: Not drawn: the {inside} inside this one. Your program’s tree is too deep to draw in full.

node.module.subject: node
node.module.title: Your program
node.module.text: The biggest box is the whole program. It holds a list of your program’s statements, {statements} in all. Python calls this box a **Module**.

node.functionDef.subject: node
node.functionDef.title: Define a function
node.functionDef.text: Everything from **def** to the end of its indented block. It has a name, **{name}**, a list of what it takes, and its own list of statements, {statements} in all. Defining it doesn’t run it. Python calls this box a **FunctionDef**.

node.arguments.subject: node
node.arguments.title: What it takes
node.arguments.text: The list of what {function} takes. Python calls this box **arguments**. It doesn’t match any single piece of your code.

node.argOnly.subject: node
node.argOnly.title: One input
node.argOnly.text: The one input {function} takes: **{name}**. When {function} is called, whatever it is given gets this name, inside {function} only. Python calls this an **arg**.

node.arg.subject: node
node.arg.title: One input
node.arg.text: One of the inputs {function} takes: **{name}**. When {function} is called, what it is given for this input gets this name, inside {function} only. Python calls this an **arg**.

node.expr.subject: node
node.expr.title: One statement
node.expr.text: A statement that does something and doesn’t keep the answer, which is fine: nobody needs it. Python calls it an **Expr** statement.

node.call.subject: node
node.call.title: Call a function
node.call.text: A call has two parts: what to call, and what to give it. This one calls **{func}**. Python calls this box a **Call**.

node.name.subject: node
node.name.title: A name
node.name.text: Just a name for now: **{name}**. Python doesn’t know yet what it points to. It looks the name up when the program runs. Python calls this a **Name**.

node.nameStore.subject: node
node.nameStore.title: A name
node.nameStore.text: The name **{name}** is given a value here. Python calls this a **Name** being stored.

node.nameStoreLoop.subject: node
node.nameStoreLoop.title: A name
node.nameStoreLoop.text: The name **{name}** is given a value each trip round the loop. Python calls this a **Name** being stored.

node.constantText.subject: node
node.constantText.title: A fixed value
node.constantText.text: A fixed value typed straight into your code: **{value}**. The quote marks are gone; they only marked where the text starts and ends. Python calls this a **Constant**.

node.constant.subject: node
node.constant.title: A fixed value
node.constant.text: A fixed value typed straight into your code: **{value}**. Python calls this a **Constant**.

node.for.subject: node
node.for.title: A loop
node.for.text: Everything from **for** to the end of its indented block. It has a name each item gets (**{target}**), something to go through (**{iter}**) and what to do each time ({statements}). Python calls this box a **For**.

node.list.subject: node
node.list.title: A list
node.list.text: The list **{code}**, with its {items}. Python calls this box a **List**.

node.assign.subject: node
node.assign.title: Store a value
node.assign.text: Python works out the value on the right of the **=**, then stores it in **{target}**, on the left. Python calls this box an **Assign**.

node.binOp.subject: node
node.binOp.title: A calculation
node.binOp.text: Two values with an operator between them, **{operator}**. Python works out the answer when the program runs. Python calls this box a **BinOp**, short for “binary operation”: an operation on two values. It calls the operator **{op}**.

node.if.subject: node
node.if.title: A choice
node.if.text: It has a test, **{test}**. If the test is true, Python runs the {statements} indented under it. If not, it moves on to the **elif** or **else** part, if there is one. Python calls this box an **If**.

node.return.subject: node
node.return.title: Hand back an answer
node.return.text: It ends the function and hands an answer back to whoever called it: what comes after **return**, or None if nothing does. Python calls this box a **Return**.

node.attribute.subject: node
node.attribute.title: A part of something
node.attribute.text: The dot reaches inside **{owner}** for something it has, called **{name}**. Python calls this an **Attribute**.

node.other.subject: node
node.other.title: Part of your program
node.other.text: Python calls this box a **{type}**. It stands for this part of your code: **{code}**.

node.otherNoPlace.subject: node
node.otherNoPlace.title: Part of the structure
node.otherNoPlace.text: Python calls this box a **{type}**. It doesn’t match any single piece of your code.

field.call.keywords.subject: node
field.call.keywords.text: what to give it, by name

terminal.cutShort.subject: program
terminal.cutShort.text: Your program ran too long to record in full. The app records up to 2,000 steps of a run, so the record of yours stops partway. Everything it printed is above.

tryIt.observed.subject: program
tryIt.observed.text: Your browser’s Python did what this command does, on your program, just now.

tryIt.nothingPrinted.subject: program
tryIt.nothingPrinted.text: Nothing: your program doesn’t print anything, so the terminal shows nothing either.

tryIt.level1.printed.subject: program
tryIt.level1.printed.text: Each line here is a line your program printed, in order.

tryIt.level1.error.subject: program
tryIt.level1.error.text: Your program stopped with an error. The last line names the error and says what went wrong; the lines above it say where. The path is where your browser’s Python saved {file}. On your computer, you’ll see your own folder.

tryIt.level2.multiByte.subject: byte
tryIt.level2.multiByte.text: Numbers from 128 to 255 come in groups of 2 to 4. [[utf8|UTF-8]] stores each character beyond English letters and common symbols that way: **{char}** is {charBytes}.

tryIt.level3.tokens.subject: program
tryIt.level3.tokens.text: After ENCODING, each line is one of the tokens at this zoom level, in the same order.

tryIt.tokenRow.encoding.subject: program
tryIt.tokenRow.encoding.text: Not a place in your file: Python’s note of the [[encoding|encoding]] it read your bytes with.

tryIt.tokenRow.position.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.position.text: Line {line}, {columns}. In each pair, the first number is the line and the second is the column. The end is the first column after the token. Columns count from 0.

tryIt.tokenRow.newline.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.newline.text: The end of a complete line of code.

tryIt.tokenRow.indent.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.indent.text: The {indent} at the start of line {line}: a block starts here.

tryIt.tokenRow.nl.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.nl.text: Line {line}’s newline is an NL, not a NEWLINE: it ends a line on the screen, but not a line of code.

tryIt.tokenRow.dedent.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.dedent.text: An empty token: a block has ended, because line {line} starts further left.

tryIt.tokenRow.dedentAtEnd.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.dedentAtEnd.text: An empty token: a block has ended, because the file has.

tryIt.tokenRow.endmarker.subject: token
tryIt.tokenRow.endmarker.text: The file has ended, so the token is empty.

tryIt.level4.boxes.subject: program
tryIt.level4.boxes.text: Each name followed by brackets, such as **Call(…)**, is one of the boxes at this zoom level, in the same order. The exceptions are **Load()**, **Store()** and **Del()**, and operators such as **Add()** or **Lt()**: each says what the box around it does.

tryIt.level4.indent.subject: program
tryIt.level4.indent.text: The indentation shows which box sits inside which.

tryIt.astRow.module.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.module.text: Your program. **body** is its list of statements: here, {statements}.

tryIt.astRow.functionDef.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.functionDef.text: The function: its name, what it takes, and its own list of statements.

tryIt.astRow.for.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.for.text: The loop: **target** is the name each item gets, **iter** is what to go through, **body** is what to do each time.

tryIt.astRow.expr.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.expr.text: One statement. **value** is what it does.

tryIt.astRow.call.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.call.text: A call: **func** is what to call, and **args** is what to give it.

tryIt.astRow.nameLoad.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.nameLoad.text: A name: **id** is the name itself. **ctx=Load()** means the name is read.

tryIt.astRow.nameStore.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.nameStore.text: A name being stored: **ctx=Store()** means the name is given a value.

tryIt.astRow.constant.subject: node
tryIt.astRow.constant.text: A fixed value: **value** is the value, as Python writes it.

1.intro: Save your program in a file called {file}, open a [[terminal|terminal]] in the same folder, and type:

parts.text: Start Python. On Windows you can also type py.
The file for Python to run.

read: Type your program exactly as it is here, with the same spaces, and press Enter after the last line before you save. Then your file holds the same {bytes} that zoom level 2 shows.

2.intro: Ask Python to show the numbers stored in your file:

parts.text: Run the small piece of Python inside the quotes, without making a new file.
Open your file. **r** means read it, **b** means as raw bytes, not as text.
Turn the bytes into a list of ordinary numbers.

read: Some Windows editors end each line with two bytes, 13 then 10. If yours does, your list has a 13 before every 10.

3.intro: Ask Python’s tokenizer to list the tokens it finds in your file:

parts.text: Run **tokenize**, the tokenizer that comes with Python, as a program.

4.intro: Ask Python to print the structure of your file as text:

parts.text: Run **ast**, Python’s module for the structure of code, as a program.
